story_type: missile defense intercept test, target air-dropped then THAAD launch
hook: A target missile dropped from a plane. They had to shoot it down.
narration: A target missile was dropped out of a plane. These soldiers had to shoot it down.
In August twenty nineteen, it fell from the back of an aircraft over the Pacific under a cluster of parachutes.
It was standing in for a medium range ballistic missile.
On Kwajalein Atoll, Army soldiers ran the radar and launchers the way they would in combat, and they did not know when the target would launch.
THAAD has no warhead. It kills a missile by hitting it.
[short pause] It was also the first time THAAD fired from a remote launcher kit, stretching the area it could defend.
outcome: The target was intercepted, THAAD's sixteenth hit in sixteen attempts.
title: Target missile dropped, then shot down
description:
Soldiers of E-62 Battery, 69th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, fire a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor from the Reagan Test Site at Kwajalein Atoll during Flight Test THAAD-23, Aug. 30, 2019.

question_comment: Would you trust a missile that has to hit another missile head on?

extra_sources.excerpt: Preliminary indications are that planned flight test objectives were achieved and the target was successfully intercepted by the THAAD weapon system.
The test, designated Flight Test THAAD (FTT)-23, was the first time the THAAD system used a government-developed remote launcher kit that extended the range of the defended area.

Soldiers from the E-62 Battery conducted radar operations, launcher and fire control operations using the same procedure they would use during combat. Simulating a real-world scenario, soldiers were unaware of the target-launch timing.
This was the 16th successful intercept in 16 attempts for the THAAD weapon system, which is designed to intercept threats both inside and outside the Earth’s atmosphere.
